t: If the blood of the bull etc.. Since the incense is to be burned after the bull is slaughtered, if the bull's blood was spilled and another bull must be slaughtered and the sprinklings begun again (as explained above in halachot 5-7), one must also take a further handful of incense in order to burn it again after the bull's slaughter.

And he takes a handful of the incense a second time before the slaughter of the bull. From the Rambam here it appears that the handful is taken before the bull is slaughtered. However, it was already explained (above, halacha 2) that they would first slaughter the bull and afterwards take the handful. The Kesef Mishneh and others emended the text and wrote that the reading should be "after the slaughter of the bull." Other commentators left the text as it is but explained that it means he takes the handful only after the bull's slaughter (see Orah VeSimchah). Rabbi Yehoshua HaNagid wrote that in this case (where he already slaughtered the first bull and took the handful after it) the handful may be taken even before the slaughter (Responsa of Rabbi Yehoshua HaNagid, no. 66, cited in the Kesef Mishneh; and see Chesed LeAvraham, who explained similarly).

He does not render garments impure, and it is not burned at the Beit HaDeshen etc.. The bull and the goat were burned outside Jerusalem at the Beit HaDeshen (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:4), and whoever touches them or carries them from the time they leave the wall of the Temple courtyard becomes impure and renders impure the garments he touches them with (Hilchot Parah 5:4-5). Since the blood of the first bull was spilled, these laws do not apply to it, and it is burned within the courtyard like other disqualified sanctified animals (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:3).
Before he finishes the sprinklings etc.. Before he finishes the sprinklings that he sprinkles from the blood of the bull and the blood of the goat separately (above 4:2).

He gives one above and seven below for the bull etc.. He continues to sprinkle from the mixed blood the applications of the bull and the applications of the goat until he completes one above and seven below for the bull, and after them one above and seven below for the goat. Every sprinkling he sprinkles contains both blood of the bull and blood of the goat, and therefore when he intends it for the bull the sprinklings count for the bull, and when he intends it for the goat the sprinklings count for the goat.

They became mixed at the last application etc.. Before he sprinkled the last sprinkling from the blood of the bull. In this case (and likewise in the other cases where the blood became mixed after the bull's sprinklings had begun) there is no need to start again from the beginning of the sequence; it is enough that he sprinkle the last application from the mixture for the bull.

And some of the cups became mixed and the cup of the bull's blood is not known etc.. One cup of the bull and one cup of the goat are known, and the two other cups are not known to be of the bull or of the goat.

And those cups that became mixed are to be poured into the channel. They are to be poured into the water channel in the Temple, like other blood found in the courtyard that drains there (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:11-12).
The Omnipresent has relinquished His ownership etc.. The Holy One, blessed be He, made all the kohanim partners as owners in this bull (see also Hilchot Temurah 1:10).

A sin offering whose owners died is to die etc.. A sin offering animal whose owners died is not offered, and its law is that it must die (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1). But since all the kohanim are partners in the Yom Kippur bull, even if the High Priest dies the sin offering is not considered a sin offering whose owners died.
In appearance, in height and in price. In general appearance, in size and in monetary value.
And their purchase as one. He should buy both of them together.

And he shall cast lots over them as at the beginning. He casts lots to choose which of them will be the partner of the goat that did not die, since a goat cannot be taken without a lottery (see above 3:3).

And the second... shall graze until it develops a blemish etc.. Since it was consecrated as an offering, it must be redeemed. They wait until it develops a blemish so that it can be redeemed by sale, and the sale proceeds are given to the collection boxes from which voluntary burnt offerings are bought.

For a communal sin offering does not die. If the goat were an individual's sin offering, its law would be to die, like a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement through another; but this law does not apply to a communal sin offering (for the laws of the sin offering that dies see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin chapter 4).
The bull and the goat of Yom Kippur that were lost. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:2.
That they become defiled. That a blemish occurs in them.
A blemish disqualifies the scapegoat. Even though it is not offered on the altar, a blemish disqualifies it like an offering.
Even a temporary blemish. A blemish that will heal in the future; even such a blemish disqualifies the offering (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:5).
Lacking in time. A disqualification that is not in the animal's body but relates to the time of its offering (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 18:8).

For example, one whose mother was slaughtered for a sick person on Yom Kippur etc.. An animal whose mother was slaughtered on the same day is forbidden to be slaughtered and is disqualified as an offering until the next day (Hilchot Shechitah 12:1). Although generally the prohibition applies only to slaughter and not to killing in other ways (ibid. 12:3), pushing the goat to Azazel is considered like slaughter, and is forbidden.
A treifah. An animal that is about to die because of a defect or a wound and the like.
He mounts it on his shoulder. Even though it is forbidden to carry on Yom Kippur (Hilchot Shevitat Asor 1:2).
He enters the Temple and takes it. Even though it is forbidden for an impure person to enter the Temple.
And he shall kill it in any way that kills it. He may kill it in any manner he wishes.
It was diminished. It was lessened.
As it says, "in the Tent of Meeting". And a tent without a roof is not a tent (this verse was said regarding the inner sprinklings of the bull of the anointed kohen).
An altar that was not inaugurated with incense. On which incense was never burned (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:1).

One of its ingredients. The incense was composed of eleven ingredients (Hilchot Kli HaMikdash 2:2); if one of them is missing, the incense is deficient and whoever burns it is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (ibid. 2:8).

Or the smoke-raiser. In addition to the ingredients of the incense, they would add to it a herb that caused its smoke to rise like a staff. If it was not added to the incense, one who burns it is liable to death, since this causes the High Priest to appear before God in the Holy of Holies without the incense cloud rising.

He is liable to death for his entry without a mitzvah. For this is the law of the High Priest: if he enters the Holy of Holies not for the sake of a mitzvah, he is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (see Hilchot Biat HaMikdash 2:3).

Therefore, if he entered inadvertently and burned deliberately, or etc.. Although he has no liability for entering without need, since he was inadvertent, or he also brought in complete incense, he is liable for the deficient incense if he burned it.
Taking a handful of the incense is a service, and intention disqualifies it etc.. Just as intention disqualifies in the service of an offering (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 13:1).
For the preparations of an offering are like the offering. Even though the placing of the coals is not a service, intention disqualifies it, since it is a preparatory act for the burning.

He took a handful with the tips of his fingers. In taking the handful of incense, the kohen would bury his palms in the incense, bring his hands together and gather up the incense. If he did not bury his hands in the incense but rested his palms on the incense and gathered it with his fingers.
From the sides. He put the incense into his palms from the sides using his thumbs.
From below upward. He placed the back of his hand on the incense and raised the incense into his hands with his fingers.
Or he took a handful with this hand and with that hand and brought them together. He took a handful with his two hands separately and then joined them together.
